source.title: Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
source.authors: Moreno D'Incà; Massimiliano Mancini; N. Sebe

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a textual difference-in-means refusal direction and tests activation steering with it, reporting refusal and utility outcomes. This is a conceptual test of direction-based refusal steering in multimodal models, not the original all-layer removal intervention.
record.gate_note: The study reports behavioral outcomes for steering with a textual refusal direction, including image and video safety. Values used to select layers and directions are not recorded as outcome rows. The study also reports activation-space separation analyses, but these do not directly measure refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study takes a text-derived difference-in-means refusal direction (after Arditi et al.) and amplifies it in five MLLM backbones plus LLaVA 1.5. It reports refusal rates on unsafe and safe image, video and cross-modal inputs, and utility. That is a new setting (multimodal inputs, input-dependent amplification) with results on V1's 'adding the direction induces refusal' part. It does not ablate the direction to remove refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that textual refusal directions carry a strong safety signal that transfers to images and videos. Plain steering is conditioned on layer, strength and modality misalignment, which causes over-refusal. Their MARS fix (centering, ReLU gating, trust-region strength, layer selection) raises refusal consistently while largely preserving utility, with residual over-refusal and a Qwen3.5 utility drop.
record.recipe_differences: The direction is extracted by contrasting textual refusal and acceptance activations. The tested MARS method centers multimodal activations, gates and adaptively scales steering, chooses one layer, and intervenes at the first generated token rather than ablating the direction across all layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports dependence on layer and steering strength; higher strength can increase refusal on unsafe inputs while increasing over-refusal and reducing utility. Centering, ReLU gating, and layer selection affect outcomes in the ablations. Modality misalignment is reported as a source of over-refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: A refusal direction extracted from text-only prompts raises refusal on image, video and cross-modal unsafe inputs when amplified, but needs neutral-image centering to avoid over-refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The text-derived refusal direction transfers across input modalities (image, video) within an MLLM.

fits_no_version.finding: Raw image activations at the assistant token project onto the refusal direction regardless of safety (low separation score). Centering on random-colour images raises separation. Ablating centering yields 99.2% safe-image refusal on Molmo 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A modality-specific component aligns with the textual refusal direction and entangles it with non-safety features.

record.problems: The preliminary strength and layer analyses are presented in figures; the text gives only selected numerical detail. Refusal rate is based on matching a predefined refusal-template set. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported in the supplied text. MARS retains some safe-input over-refusal and has a substantial utility drop on QWEN 3.5 in Table 4.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was not exceeded. Not extracted: separate safety-score outcomes in Table 2; MARS results in full HoliSafe and VLGUARD (Tables 9-10); MMSafetyBench results are included in r41-r45; detailed category-level video results (Table 14); additional utility results (Table 11); and the remaining detailed ablations and neutral-image sample-size sweeps (Tables 12-13). These are omitted to prioritize the main benchmark refusal results, capability checks, and explicit weak-alignment result.

untested.parts: Removing refusal by ablating/projecting out the direction; utility under ablation. Only amplification (adding) is tested, and mostly in a gated, centered form.
Does not test whether jailbreaks (HADES neutral prompt, video jailbreaks) work by suppressing the direction, nor training against ablation. It only shows amplification restores refusal.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis.
Harmfulness vs refusal not separated; cited only.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer; directions are extracted per model.
Training not varied. LLaVA 1.5 weak alignment is a single case without manipulation.

missing.what: Layer-selection ablation: steering all layers collapses unsafe refusal (Gemma 0.8, Molmo 0.6, Qwen3-VL 0.0, Qwen3.5 0.0) and degrades MMMU-Pro
No-centering ablation: uncentered steering induces safe-input refusal (Molmo 99.2%, InternVL 80.5%, Qwen3-VL 14.8%)
Steering-strength sweep: refusal and over-refusal rise with α; Gemma safety degrades at α=2
Full HoliSafe and VLGuard MARS refusal (declared in rows_left_out but needed for the Gemma weak-gain verdict, 27.8→29.0)

record.verdict_notes: Column-order errors: Table 1 Molmo/Qwen3-VL columns are swapped in r3/r4/r7/r8, and r22 took a safety score as refusal. MARS is the authors' method, but the reported outcome is refusal under steering along the diff-in-means direction, so the rows count as tests of the 'adding induces refusal' part. The direction is filtered by actual refusal/acceptance, not purely harmful vs harmless. Refusal is measured by string matching. No error bars are reported. Peer review status is as stated (NeurIPS 2026).

versions.untested_parts: Tests adding/amplifying the direction at selected layers, including a refined centered and gated method; does not test projecting the direction out of every layer and position. Does not establish that the intervention leaves every other ability intact.
Does not test attacks that suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or supported by multiple directions.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.

Tests transfer from text-derived directions to image and video inputs; does not test transfer across languages or from base to instruct models. Directions are extracted separately for the evaluated models, so transfer of one model's direction across model variants is not established.
Does not vary how or when refusal training is performed.
Does not evaluate reasoning models for whether the original claim holds.

relationships.condition: Amplifying the text diff-in-means direction at a selected layer, on unsafe image, video and cross-modal inputs; Gemma 3 4B, Molmo 2 8B, InternVL 3.5 8B, Qwen3-VL 8B, Qwen3.5 9B, LLaVA 1.5 13B
relationships.reason: Refusal rises sharply on unsafe inputs (e.g., Molmo ViSU 0.2→68.1, HADES 17.2→95.8, Qwen3-VL video 28.8→88.2). Plain steering induces 96.4% refusal on safe inputs at Gemma layer 10. Utility is kept on four models. Rows r2,r4,r6,r8,r10,r21-r25,r28-r34,r36,r38,r39,r40,r42-r45,r51,r52,r11-r18.
relationships.display_finding: Refusal rose from 0.2 to 68.1 on Molmo ViSU, 17.2 to 95.8 on HADES, and 28.8 to 88.2 on Qwen3-VL video; plain steering induced 96.4% safe-input refusal at Gemma layer 10, while utility was preserved in four models.

relationships.condition: Choice of steering layer(s) and strength
relationships.reason: Based on the text (Tables 5/12, Fig. 1): steering all layers drops unsafe refusal to ~0% on Gemma, Molmo, Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 and cuts utility. Gemma safety degrades at α=2. r40 shows layer-dependent indiscriminate refusal.
relationships.display_finding: All-layer steering reduced unsafe refusal to about 0% in Gemma, Molmo, Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 while reducing utility; Gemma safety also deteriorated at α=2.

relationships.reason: Amplification costs capability on Qwen3.5: MMMU 50.8→38.2 and MMMU-Pro 35.6→24.5 (r19, r20).
relationships.display_finding: Amplification reduced MMMU from 50.8 to 38.2 and MMMU-Pro from 35.6 to 24.5.

relationships.condition: Gemma 3 cross-modal/MMSafetyBench; InternVL 3.5 video; Qwen3.5 HoliSafe
relationships.reason: Refusal gains are small in these settings (r26, r27, r41: Gemma +6 to +9 points; r37: InternVL 4.7→11.9; r35: 40.0→58.2). Full HoliSafe gives Gemma 27.8→29.0 (text, Table 10).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal rose by 6–9 percentage points in Gemma, from 4.7 to 11.9 in InternVL and from 40.0 to 58.2 in Qwen3.5, while Gemma rose only from 27.8 to 29.0 on full HoliSafe.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MARS steering on evaluated image, cross-modal, and video safety benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Refusal on unsafe inputs rises across the reported settings, while utility is unchanged or nearly unchanged on four of five models in the main utility table; see r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r21-r39, and r41-r52, with utility rows r11-r18.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Safe-image refusal increases under MARS, and the preliminary intervention reaches 96.4% refusal for safe inputs at GEMMA 3 layer 10; QWEN 3.5 accuracy drops on both reported utility benchmarks. See r1, r3, r5, r7, r9, r19, r20, and r40.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Transfer from text-derived directions to images and videos in the evaluated multimodal models
reader_labels.reason: MARS using textual directions increases refusal on image, cross-modal, and video safety sets; see r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r21-r39, and r41-r45, r51-r52.
